title: Family Recipe Book
goal: Your kid collects recipes from the people in your family, asks them for the stories behind the food, cooks each dish from their own notes, and writes it up so anyone could make it. It all goes into a little cookbook with their name on the cover. The test is real: if the dish doesn't come out right, the writing needs fixing.
create: 3 to 5 family recipes, each with the story behind it
Recipe cards written so someone outside the family could cook from them
A mini cookbook with a cover, a table of contents and their name on it
need: Family or friends willing to share a favourite recipe, in person, by phone or on video
A notebook for interview notes, and your kitchen and ingredients
For the taste detective: one family dish everyone loves, homemade or leftovers

lesson.text: Good recipe writing gives three things at every step: the exact amount, the exact action, and a sign you can see when it's done. Family cooks skip all three because they just know. Your kid's job is to write them down.
lesson.before: Add some flour. Mix it a bit. Bake until done.

model.line: Add 2 cups of flour, one cup at a time.
Stir with a wooden spoon until you can't see any dry flour.
It's ready when the top is golden and springs back when you press it.

lesson.modelNote: A family cook reads 'some' and 'until done' and just knows. A stranger needs a number, an action and a sign they can see.

howTo.intro: You handle the hot and sharp parts. When the notes say 'some flour', don't quietly add the right amount: let the gap show so it ends up on the card.

plan.what: The taste detective game, then choose the recipes (Step 1). About 20 minutes.
Interview the cooks, then cook one recipe at a time from the notes (Steps 2 and 3).
Write the recipe cards and put the book together (Steps 4 and 5).

troubleshoot.a: A video call works great. Ask the cook to show each step on camera while your kid takes notes.
That's useful. Something is missing from the notes. Call the cook back and ask about that exact step.
Ask them to cook while your kid catches each handful or splash in a measuring cup or spoon before it goes in, and writes it down.

fromHome.text: Our kids each have a dish that's theirs now: my daughter's chili and my son's smashburgers. We also eat a pasta everyone calls Mamie's pastas, and their grand-maman makes a hazelnut cake, le gâteau aux avelines, that the kids ask for every single birthday.

skills.text: writing instructions someone else can follow without help

skills.name: Interviewing
skills.text: asking good questions and listening for the details

skills.name: Real-world math

steps.title: Play taste detective
steps.why: Tasting a dish everyone loves gets your kid asking how it's made, and that's where the book starts.
steps.kid: Your kid picks a family dish everyone loves and tastes it slowly, one bite at a time. They write down every ingredient they think is in it, and how they think it's made. The cook's recipe will settle it in the interview. Then they make a list of dishes that mean something to your family and pick 3 to 5, ideally from different people.
steps.you: Serve the dish (leftovers work) and play along: write your own guesses and compare who got closer once the cook tells you. Then help them think of family dishes and who makes them, and let them choose. Try to include someone they don't talk to often.
ask: What do you taste that you didn't expect?
If we could only save 5 recipes from our family, which would they be?
steps.tip: Mix everyday food and special occasions. The Tuesday spaghetti belongs in the book as much as the holiday dinner.

levels.explore: Guess 3 ingredients in the mystery dish, then pick 2 or 3 family recipes and who they come from.
levels.develop: Guess every ingredient and one step of how it's made, then pick 3 or 4 recipes from different people.
levels.extend: Guess the amounts by ratio too: more flour than sugar? About twice as much? Check your ratios in the interview.

steps.title: Interview the cooks
steps.why: Your kid gets each recipe, and the story behind it, straight from the cook.
steps.kid: Your kid talks to the person who makes each dish, in person, by phone or on video. They ask for the ingredients and the steps, how long things take, and any secret tricks. Then they ask where the recipe came from and what memory goes with it. They write down both. For the taste-detective dish, they compare their guesses with the cook's list.
steps.you: Set up the conversations, then let your kid do the asking. Practise a couple of questions together before the first call. When the cook says 'a pinch' or 'until it looks right,' nudge your kid to ask what that means.
ask: What's the one thing that makes this dish turn out right?
Who taught you this recipe, and how?
steps.tip: If the cook says something memorable, write down their exact words. Those make the best recipe introductions.

levels.explore: Ask for the recipe and write down the ingredients and basic steps.
levels.develop: Ask about both the recipe and the story behind it, and take notes on both.
levels.extend: Ask the cook to make it while you watch, and write down every step they do but didn't mention.

steps.title: Cook it from the notes
steps.why: The real test: can your kid make the dish from what they wrote down?
steps.kid: Your kid cooks each recipe using only their notes, with your help where needed. As they go, they mark anything unclear or missing: a step the cook forgot, an amount like 'some,' something the cook does by feel. They write down the real amounts, temperatures and times as they find them.
steps.you: Handle the hot and sharp parts and let your kid lead everything else. When they get stuck, don't fill the gap from your own cooking. Ask what the notes say, and help them work out what's missing.
ask: What did the heat change: did something melt, rise, thicken or brown? That's the sign for the card.
Where would someone who's never made this get stuck?
steps.tip: A dish that flops isn't a failure. It shows exactly where the notes need more detail, and it's a great excuse to call the cook back.

levels.explore: Cook one recipe while a grown-up reads the notes aloud. Add a sticker each time you ask 'how much?' or 'how long?'
levels.develop: Cook 2 or 3 recipes, mark every gap, and add exact amounts and times.
levels.extend: When a step says 'a handful', measure one 3 times and write down the middle amount.

steps.title: Write the recipe cards
steps.why: Your kid turns the notes into recipe cards a stranger could follow.
steps.kid: Your kid writes a card for each dish, all in the same format: the name, who it comes from, a short story or quote, the ingredients with exact amounts, and numbered steps. Every step gets an action and a sign it's done, plus an amount whenever something goes in, like the example at the start. Then they read each card out loud and fix anything vague.
steps.you: Read each card as if you've never made the dish. Could you cook it from this alone? Point out one or two spots that would trip you up, then let your kid fix them.
ask: Could a friend make this without calling you?
How would someone know when this step is done?
steps.tip: List the ingredients in the order they get used. It's the first thing a cook checks.

levels.explore: Draw each step in its own box, in order, and add the amounts with a grown-up.
levels.develop: Write detailed cards with exact amounts, clear steps and a short story, then have someone read one and revise.
levels.extend: Rescale one recipe to serve 2 or 12, and flag what doesn't scale neatly, like one egg or a pinch of salt.

steps.title: Make the cookbook and share it
steps.why: The cards become a real book, and it goes back to the people who shared their recipes.
steps.kid: Your kid puts the cards together into a cookbook: a cover with a title and their name, a table of contents, and the recipes in an order that makes sense (by person, by meal, or easy to hard). Then they give copies to the family, especially the cooks who shared their recipes.
steps.you: Help with printing or stapling, but let them decide how it looks and what goes where. This is their book. When it's done, be the first reader and tell them which page you love most.
ask: Who would you dedicate this book to?
What did you learn about our family that you didn't know before?
steps.tip: When a grandparent opens the book and sees their own recipe in their grandkid's writing, that's the moment this whole project was for.

levels.explore: Put the recipes together with a cover and your name, and give it to one family member.
levels.develop: Add a table of contents and a short introduction about your family's food, and share it with the cooks.
levels.extend: Give one card to someone outside the family to cook alone. Note every question they ask, and fix the card before it goes in.

conclusion.headline: 'A bit of this' is written down properly now.
conclusion.text: Hand them a recipe from a website or an old recipe box and have them read one step aloud. Watch for them catching a vague word or a missing sign that it's done. They can tell you why 'bake until done' isn't really an instruction.
conclusion.celebrate: When the dish they cooked from their own notes tastes like the cook's version, say it: 'That tastes just like theirs, and your notes got it there.'
extensions: Keep adding recipes and make a second volume
Cook a whole family meal from the book, start to finish
Make a holiday edition with the dishes your family only cooks once a year
Interview someone from a different generation or background about their food
Photograph each dish and make a photo cookbook

signs: They check amounts and times before cooking
They catch vague words in recipes ('some,' 'a bit,' 'until done')
They want to cook from the book on their own
makeItReal: Cook one recipe from the book for the person who shared it, and serve it with their recipe card on the table. Or bring copies to the next family gathering and let someone cook from one.
cta: Want the next one? This guide is one of 120+ in the Anywhere Learning library, each with your job and your kid's job at every step.
levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

Buy the ingredients for one local recipe at the market, and find out what each one is called here.
Cook a recipe in your rental kitchen with whatever pans and measures it has, and rewrite the amounts to match.
backHome: Cook one dish from the trip for the family at home, and add its card to the book with the story behind it.
